lessons.title: READ
intro: A program that only works with numbers punched into it isn't much use. READ (5,10) I, J takes the next card from the card reader, unit 5, and reads the values the way FORMAT 10 describes.
The data cards went into the reader behind the program deck. To run the same program with new numbers, you only punched new data cards. The program stayed the same.
FORMAT (2I5) means: two integers, five columns each. The first comes from columns 1–5, the second from columns 6–10.

exercises.prompt: Which unit is the card reader?
exercises.explanation: Unit 5 reads, unit 6 prints. You'll see READ (5, …) and WRITE (6, …) in FORTRAN programs for decades.

exercises.prompt: Why keep data on separate cards instead of in the program?
options: The same program can run again with new data
exercises.explanation: Punch the program once, then feed it as many data decks as you like.

exercises.prompt: Read one integer from the card reader.
A data card holds "   12   30". What does READ (5,10) I, J with FORMAT (2I5) store?
This job stops with *ERROR*. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: Unit 6 is the printer. You can't read from a printer: it has to be READ (5,10).

exercises.prompt: Where do the data cards go?
options: Inside the program, after each READ
exercises.explanation: The compiler reads the program, then the running program takes the cards that come after it.

lessons.title: Columns Count
intro: On a data card, the format decides which columns belong to which number. F6.2 reads six columns. If there's no decimal point on the card, FORTRAN puts one in itself: "  1250" read with F6.2 becomes 12.50. That saved punching the points.
Careful with blanks: inside a field, a blank counts as a zero. "42   " read with I5 isn't 42, it's 42000. Numbers had to be punched right-aligned in their columns.
Mistakes like these were classic. A shifted card could turn a measurement into nonsense without any error message.

exercises.prompt: A card holds "  1250", read with F6.2. What value is stored?
exercises.explanation: No decimal point on the card, so the format puts it 2 places from the right.

exercises.prompt: A card holds "42   ", read with I5. What value is stored?
exercises.explanation: The three blanks after 42 count as zeros. Numbers belong at the right end of their field.
When the card has a decimal point, it wins over the format.

exercises.prompt: Read an integer from columns 1–3 and a real number from columns 4–9.
exercises.explanation: After I3 come six more columns: F6.2.

exercises.prompt: The card says "   7   9" but J comes out as 90. Which card is wrong?
exercises.explanation: I5 reads columns 5–9, but the 9 sits in column 8. The blank in column 9 counts as a zero, so J becomes 90. FORMAT (2I4) matches the card.

exercises.prompt: Why did programmers draw the card layout on paper before punching data?
options: Every number has to sit in exactly the right columns
exercises.explanation: Coding sheets with 80 little boxes per line were on every programmer's desk.

lessons.title: Until the Last Card
intro: Often you don't know how many data cards there will be. The trick: put a special last card with a value that can't be real data, like -1. It's called a sentinel.
The program reads in a loop. After every READ, an IF checks for the sentinel and jumps out of the loop when it comes.
Inside the loop, count the cards and add up the values, and you have everything for an average.

options: A last card with a special value that marks the end of the data
The first card of the program
A card with a C in column 1
exercises.explanation: A value like -1 or 9999 that real data never has.

exercises.prompt: In the example, why is the IF right after the READ?
options: So the sentinel itself isn't counted or added
It doesn't matter where it is
exercises.explanation: Check first, then use the value. Otherwise -1 would end up in the sum.

exercises.prompt: What happens if the sentinel card is missing?
options: The program tries to read past the last card and stops with an error
exercises.explanation: The reader runs out of cards: *ERROR* END OF DATA.
Use the same sentinel value the data deck ends with.

exercises.prompt: Stack the cards for a loop that reads values until -1 and counts them.
exercises.explanation: Read, check, count, jump back. The FORMATs can sit anywhere, but here every card has its place.

exercises.prompt: This counts one card too many. Which card is in the wrong place?
exercises.explanation: N = N + 1 runs before the sentinel check, so the -1 card gets counted too. Check first, then count.
